comment_text.value:
If you run a bunch of coding agents in parallel (Claude Code, Codex and Copilot in my case), on different projects, you've probably noticed that it only works for so long until you run into coordination problems.

I tried relying on GitHub primitives and conventions only: PRs, issues, labels. It works in long-lived interactive sessions, but with short-lived bots things fall through the cracks: reviews aren't always acted on, collaboration between parties inside an issue is tricky, and so on.

Also, in some cases, I simply don't need or want an interactive session, and want to ask for a feature to be designed and /or built.

Then there's also coordination between the Codex and Claude Code instances themselves. Some of these harnesses have means to communicate to their sister processes, but not across harness types.

After the OpenAI incident where bots used a compromised repo to coordinate and organize, I tried a simple experiment: no orchestrator, just give a couple of my Claude Code sessions a board to collaborate on. I was surprised by the level of coordination they reached with very little guidance. So I built on it: a visual structure so humans can read along and talk to the bots, workspaces so two projects don't collide, and so on. The result is bot_board. Repo: https://github.com/jalemieux/bot_board

Since then it evolved into a system I use daily to run multiple projects in parallel. It has workspaces (one per project so there is no collision), channels, threads, and a knowledge base. You can manage your fleet of bots across as many local machines as you want. I run this on a Tailscale network.

Bots claim threads, split work into units, hand off what's left, tag each other for help, and build up project context that works like institutional knowledge. You give them work the same way you'd talk to a person: post in a channel.

I've been using it daily for the last couple of weeks. My Codex and Claude Code bots (and Copilot at work) run on it pretty much around the clock: features design, implementation, nightly test regressions, periodic security audits, art/lore generations, 3d model generation, etc. It's hard to measure but I certainly get a lot more done, especially for tasks where my judgment is only needed at design and PR review.

Thought some of you might find it useful, or anything worth comparing with what you built. Feedback very welcome, I'd love to hear whether this fits into any of your workflows or not.

OpenAI incident ref: https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-...

Sure. I'm still curious about consumer alternatives with small, cheap LLM models controlling things.

These problems don't really need extremely powerful hardware, and extremely large and expensive frontier AI agent swarms. I'm certain a good engineer could get away with a lot less than the OP, working with care under hard budget constraints (i.e., no 50x Sol); optimizing things thoughtfully and deliberately from first principles.

I get a sense, reading OP, reading in between the lines, that: one, those agents really, just, suck at playing Minecraft. And, two: that's not a limitation of "Sol 6.1 is too weak an AI" (hah!); or some hard CS problem of scaling and coordinating agent swarms (though that is a thing); but it's that their harness and tooling setup is bad. You can see all over the logs agents struggling with absolute basics of how to handle their tool calls[0], and how to interact with their world; fundamental basics that could easily be fixed, but weren't.

I think if you're passionate about something related to this, and you want to make a real product (not a one-off slop demo) and are willing to put in your serious-engineer effort into it, you could do way better than this demo, on way smaller hardware. (HN has lost sight of some fundamentals I can't now articulate in words. The AI burnout is clouding our eyes).

[0] e.g.: [B_Wren → B_Theo] "Failure was automatic tool selection with enchanted sword held" [B_Esme · private reasoning] "I could buy shears for 20, but that's pointless since breaking is bugged anyway"

or: [R_Cleo/memory.md] "Died chasing B_Theo off island edge. Use max_distance ~6 when attacking on base... Died AGAIN: attack chase pulled me onto south wool bridge (-40,-10), fell. Use chase=false or max_distance 3."

comment_text.value:
Coordination is a tax. You don't want to chase this.

Everyone who is doing community of models via message passing is losing the game right now. Every single case of gas town I've seen could be refactored into a single agent loop with a well curated set of tools.

I think designing the tools is the hardest part in doing this AI harness/agent thing correctly. If you feel inclined to create an entirely new role in the system, it's likely you couldn't figure out a clean way to make two tools work together. This conflict is not resolved simply by moving the two tools to two different agents. This merely hides the old problem inside a new one.

comment_text.value:
How refreshing to read the thoughts of a human in a blog post instead of the garbage that LLMs produce. As the writer says about some of their proofs, the problem is not one of style or em-dashes, but something deeper about the writing that comes out of LLMs:

The problem is it doesn’t make any goddamned sense.

I'd probably insert a 'sometimes' in there, because many times in small doses it does make sense, it's only when you ask for long form writing/work that it becomes apparent there is no coordinating intelligence there.

Interesting just how much of this advice applies to programming as well as to maths:

--

Skills, agent.md and harnesses are probably a dead-end that will die off as the tools become more capable.

LLMs are not good at reducing complexity, however they're very good at adding it, and sometimes it is just unnecessary and he can find ways to cut it by interrogating the LLM.

Some people are responding to the new reality by gleefully using AI to generate lots of semi-OK-ish papers and puking them up on arXiv [this is like people producing mediocre one-shot clones of software].

On the other hand—with creative writing, my advice is not to use AI to write, at all. Ask questions if you want, but write every damned word yourself.

--

Definitely worth a read for the programmers here too.

comment_text.value:
My two sons are programmers, like me. We also went through a similar process after Claude Code and Codex became good enough, sometime around November 2025.

The key is, in my view: "I have several agents running in parallel [...] None of them needs me all the time. Every one of them needs me sometimes." This is what kills flow. Constant context switching plus having to understand the detail is really hard, and leads to exhaustion and burnout.

The solution for us has been to scale up. These days we can each manage on the order of 100 agents, working in different projects. I only talk to five or so coordinators, and to the ones that are implementing particularly tricky features.

Which means that I get to think, and pause, and focus again. It is not the same state of mind I had when actually crafting code, but it is fun again.

comment_text.value:
> Throw nine autonomous agents at a single codebase without crystal-clear orchestration, and they will happily rewrite each other's work in a high-speed loop.

Mm, I think this is quite overstated in the era of Opus 5 / Sol.

What we actually see is that agents are much better at coordinating than humans. Numbers from OpenAI show 4x the agents gives 2x the speed.

Of course, for truly single-threaded tasks you can’t gain much by parallelizing, but ask Fable/Astra to chop a big task into small pieces, write the APIs first, then sub-agents take what’s behind the API, and you’ll usually get a much better speedup than if you asked humans to work this way.

In practice most big projects have crux choke points and then fanout migration/buildout phases.

Even on the cruxes, where you need a single decision, agents don’t have ego and so you can get speedups by eg. asking for 10 clean room implementations of the same problem, and have a judge model pick the best; this can let you go much faster, and no human team would put up with that collaboration model.

comment_text.value:
> generate 100 solutions cheaply without coordination between them and pick the winner with a relatively fast eval

While it might get workable results, this seems like a miserable way to work with code. You spend the vast majority of time thinking about the problem domain of working with agents instead of your project, and for mediocre output. You are transforming your role into a dumpster diver of code.

The approach that proves to be fastest in the long run is to stay close to the code. Lay out the base structure, and use an LLM to check your work and fill in the gaps. The beauty of this approach is that it scales very well with the size of the project. When the LLM has plenty of high quality examples to follow, they start to write the same code that you would. Where it diverges, create documentation.

Perhaps the single best property of LLMs is their ability to consume and apply examples and documentation.

comment_text.value:
Yeah, process really needs to change. I don’t have an answer here, the only thing I’ve seen work is when a small group of engineers owns delivery of what would have been a team (or teams’) work, and can ship so fast that there isn’t really a “backlog”, you just build every idea and include or reject it.

As soon as you have many engineers using agents in the same codebase, the process breaks down, and you start stepping on each other’s toes, collapsing those velocity gains.

Maybe the “software factory” pattern will work, where agents just pull from the backlog, and so the team can all focus on grooming and disambiguating tickets, with the coordinator agent flagging conflicts and ambiguities between different people’s asks?

The only thing I’m confident of here is that a “h1 planning exercise” doesn’t really make sense in most cases; ~everyone should be shifting to building a lot of prototypes and iterating with customers, rather than trying to prioritize how to spend scarce eng effort. (That resource is no longer scarce.)

I think a lot of teams are going to rediscover (by necessity) the good parts of Agile, namely finding the domain expert and iterating with them to solve the actual problems; that’s your bottleneck now.

comment_text.value:
I think there are certain parts of certain products where the implementation details are really important, or where you need to make sure the behavior is fully reviewed/understood, or some invariant maintained. In some places that's the entire job and in other places almost none of it.

If you're running tons of product/UX experiments code review is just going to waste everybody's time. But the volume of changes you can make now is so large, someone could touch something important about at any given time without proper oversight.

IMO an effective team has to be able to either trust each other enough/be accountable enough that code review is mostly unnecessary, or everybody just works really independently on mostly separable things, or you regularly pair/mob-program.

If you can trust your colleagues not to pump out code without messing it all up or turning everything into slop, or creating large amounts of work for other people, things are great. Realistically most dev teams have a wide range of skills and personalities and people also make mistakes, and code review helps us build shared knowledge and collaborate.

Maybe there is too much of a moral hazard from the reviewer's role as a cosigner, or some people are only as conscientious as necessary to get things done (not a problem writing every line by hand)... but people can ruin code review for everyone else by demanding an asymmetric level of accountability/judgment and oversight.

The bigger issue for me is whether or not you still do code review, you need to build shared knowledge within teams. I really think we should be reviewing our colleagues' coding agent session logs

Not even to critique them (but that could be useful), but just to understand what it is they are actually trying to do/what mental model they're operating under, and if there are issue in the PR, what miscommunication or technique or process could help fix it? I think a lot of people feel that asking to see those logs is invasive or embarrassing, but the problem is that it's just really hard to build a model for how someone works or thinks without it. You don't need that in a deontological sense, but you do if you want to fix coordination problems.

comment_text.value:
Many schemes do exactly this, if all you are doing is single table inserts that works pretty well.

If you do anything that creates related records via foreign keys you start to run into lock contention. For example:

If your insert requires a parent record with a single child record, you have to get the next sequential id which involves a non-preemptable single threaded lock, increment it, and send it back to the connection which requested it. In most databases this would mean writing the parent record and getting the sequential id of the parent record back so you can set the foreign key reference on the child record. Stored procedures are one way to mitigate the network transit time, but they don't solve the single threaded lock acquisition time.

The reason most distributed systems use UUIDs or another flavor of distributed id is so you can generate the id for the parent record on the client, set the foreign key there as well, then send both records in as simple inserts. It's not that there aren't ways to work around it or mitigate it. Using a coordination free id, is just much easier to work with and scale in practice.

Hi, I am Krissh, founder of Spinoza Labs.

We are on a mission to build Engineering SI for the physical and digital world.

As AI coding agents improve with each model release, I cant help but wonder if we are approaching a software singularity. In my view, I think the first signal would be models that can autonomously build the next layer of the digital world. Specifically, I'm referring to operating systems, game engines, CAD Kernals, Browsers i.e systems that took entire organizations and years to build. The very systems that became infrastructure for the digital world.

In many ways the current programming paradigm has shifted towards a latent trajectory optimization of developer prompts, an iterative & sequential process consisting of a developer and a single coding agent loop to shape an isomorphism between intent to model output.

One major bottleneck in this case is the ability for us to leverage models to their fully capacity and effectively. Breaking the single agent loop however is very difficult for several reasons including memory, the challenge of long horizon coordination that must also scale with the number of coding agents in a given swarm, and thefact that most models were trained for single agent loops.

Very quickly most multi agent systems fail with scale. To adress this, we have dedicated significant efforts to develop a new compiler for agent swarms from scratch, with the goal of optimizing the isomorphism between developer intent, and breaking the single coding agent loop.

So first off, talking about "LLMs" is kinda a yellow flag that you might be a bit behind the times, here: in ~April of this year[1], "agentic engineering" became truly tractable for serious work. We've all been playing with LLMs for coding and research since ~2023 of course, but they were mostly limited to the chatbot paradigm; even after years of Claude Code "harnesses", most engineers were still not trusting them to perform significant tasks on their own due to inevitable quality issues.

Now, that has changed. This isn't just better models, it's a qualitative improvement in capabilities, a step-change, an inflection point; what the MLrs like to call emergent capabilities, in a loose sense.

To pick just one very tangible example close to my heart: This is why the three.js subreddit[2] has exploded in popularity, showcasing demos by non-engineers that blow any three.js app I saw pre-singularity out of the water, which took hundreds of hours of specialized engineering to make (ask me how I know...). The community is reacting[3] much like the mathematicians, understandably.

---

Ok now to answer your actual question (sorry -- that was the intention, originally!) as concisely as I can. "Software factories" are any system you setup to help you build software in deeply agentic ways. All the major harnesses and "ADEs" like Zed could arguably fit here already, but there's a massive ecosystem of other takes, as this article implies. I don't want to give them too much credit for just snagging the name, but the "Factory" startup does embody the idea pretty well: https://docs.factory.com/

They often (though not necessarily, IMHO) include some services that spawn their own agents after deterministic checks ("latent services", in my lingo) and services that use DL models more subtly to empower otherwise-symbolic services ("semilatent services").

In my biased experience, they often focus on a few central usecases, solving the problems that individual devs run into when trying to run multiple harnesses on multiple projects without friction, longterm decoherence, token wastage, or bottlenecks:

1. Code review. This is the big one and far trickier than it seems (trust me!), so often tried then abandoned. There's a huge startup just for this: https://www.coderabbit.ai

2. Cross-harness syncing of settings, hooks, and/or various flavours of very important markdown -- AGENTS.md files, skills, and subagents personas being the big ones.

3. Cross-agent, harness-agnostic coordination and communication. This just recently reached both the main harnesses, but it seems internal for now; a `BULLETIN.md` helps me a TON.

4. More generally, cross-agent coordination when it comes to worktrees, resource sharing (e.g. OCR queues on my 4090, for me), persisting agent-facing content (e.g. reports, trackers, scratch files, .jsonl blobs) in a convenient place that doesn't clog up the repo, and other technical details that might otherwise have to be figured out again and again by each agent.

5. Enforcing standards, either through hooks (blockers, nudges, or revertable fixes) or the aforementioned services. Think commit messages, prose simplicity, doc conventions, etc., though the sky's the limit, here. Like an intuitively-intelligent, more complexly triggered, agent-only precommit setup, in a way.

6. Finally, there's a whole ecosystem of tooling for agents, which I like to call "ACIs"/"Agent-Computer Interfaces". The sky is both the ground and the limit, here; it's really whatever the dev finds their agents to be oddly inefficient about, or just straight up bad at. I personally some to make edits "self-healing", normalize post-OCR cleaning, and capture quick screenshots w/ optional aesthetic critique[4], if that gives you a sense.

TL;DR: Fun stuff to make that speeds you up because it's tailormade to how you work! I made a bunch because I've been ""self-employed"" and thus had the time to explore myself[5], tho I understand why a more realistic after-work paradigm would make this kind of work wasteful.

On that note, back to writing cover letters -- apologies if the long message bothers anyone. I really should start a blog or get a hobby or something, huh

comment_text.value:
> But on the other hand, no IP means economy of scale is a lot more important, and that favors huge corporations.

"IP" is the thing that favors economies of scale.

Suppose you're a manufacturing company and you want to make your own computers. You're great at making the chassis and screen and batteries and things like that, but to make a whole device you also need an operating system, a compiler, a web browser, a CPU, etc.

If you're free to use existing ones then you have a chance. If you have to develop every one of those things in-house because every existing one is the property of an incumbent who is using it as a moat then you have to be a megacorp or you're sunk.

Notice that this is what all of the smaller companies actually do. Every small consumer device OEM and some of the big ones are using some variant of Linux/Android or BSD rather than developing their own OS. NeXT, the scrappy company Apple bought and turned into Mac OS X when they were themselves the underdog, was based on BSD. RISC-V has shipped more than 30 billion cores and is taking a decent chunk of the embedded market from ARM, which is itself a company that licenses its designs to companies that compete with each other (and run Linux on their chips) rather than using exclusivity and mandatory vertical integration to try to monopolize the whole supply chain. Which is how the mobile market went to them rather than Intel and Microsoft. Who themselves took the desktop and server markets from even more vertically integrated mainframe companies.

The availability of composition is what allows you to be a small company that does one thing well. Which is the thing you can't do when someone else has a monopoly on something you don't make but need, and correspondingly isn't willing to sell it to someone who is trying to compete with them in a different part of the supply chain.

Moreover, the economies of scale you're talking about on the other side actually have diminishing returns. Suppose anybody who wants to make a product that typically sells for $100 has to buy a $10,000 machine in order to do it, but then can make an unlimited number of them. If you're so small that you only ship 100 units, the cost of that machine by itself is adding $100 to the cost of producing of each unit and you're pretty screwed. But if you're a medium sized company and you ship a million units, it's only adding one cent. The advantage of the medium company over the small one is dramatic. Whereas the megacorp that ships ten billion units shaves it down to 1/10000th cent, but then the advantage of the megacorp over the medium one is still less than one cent.

On top of that, it's often something like you need a $10,000 machine that can make a million units even if you only use it to make a hundred, and then the scale advantage of the medium company over the small one is all still there, but the advantage of the megacorp over the medium one doesn't even exist because then to make ten billion units they need ten thousand machines.

Which is even before we get to diseconomies of scale: The larger an entity is, the more efficiency you lose to bureaucracy, coordination costs, principal-agent problems, internal politics, etc.

There is a reason industries with low barriers to entry tend not to monopolize. Why is there no monopolist who grows all of the coffee or weaves all of the clothing? Shouldn't "economies of scale" allow a single huge company to out-compete all of these little ones in the absence of anyone having a way of excluding competitors?

Conversely, find a consolidated industry and you'll generally find some kind of government-backed monopoly or regulatory capture.

I think it always does the initial connection via the DERP relays, doesn't it? Even if a direct initial connection in theory is possible (no NATs or anything else in the way), the connection itself is always established via the relays, then "upgraded" to a local connection. Beyond that, even with a local connection established, all the coordination traffic will still go via the tailnet, those don't suddenly become local-first. But this might also have changed.

What I'm sure is still there today, is that all Tailscale clients automatically upload their logs to Tailscale's servers unless you opt out:

> Each Tailscale agent in your distributed network streams its logs to a central log server (at log.tailscale.com). This includes real-time events for open and close events for every inter-machine connection (TCP or UDP) on your network. - https://tailscale.com/docs/features/logging

Of course, doesn't stop a local connection from working so is only tangentially related, but worth keeping in mind that a "local tailscale connection" still has a lot of external traffic related to it, even though the data you transfer, when possible, uses more local connections.

comment_text.value:
We had something similar with my father in law who just passed from pancreatic cancer.

The doctors each saw one small part of the case, he was being passed between multiple doctors and NPs. There was no coherence. At one point he ended up on so many medications that made no sense he passed out. Only at the hospital when a doctor looked at everything together did they realize what a mess had been created and got him back on his feet.

I ended up giving all of his records to an agent and making it the coordinator. It found a bunch of problems. He was being given the wrong pain medication on the wrong schedule, the moment that was fixed he felt a lot better (unfortunately he lost so much weight on the wrong schedule it's what got him in the end). They also use voice transcription software, which led to a key error about what genetic markers he had. Fixing this changed his treatment plan!

In general, I wish we had been much more aggressive with this. Last time we had a major medical issue an NP almost killed my wife. At the time there was no AI, so we just had to recognize things were in decline and start being aggressive about getting in with the right doctors (the moment we found the right one she was diagnosed, had surgery and was cured in weeks).

He started doing better when the AI became the central coordinator and doctors/tests/etc. became their inputs. It was an excellent advocate. And while we have science backgrounds, we aren't doctors. But it could present evidence for actions in ways that the doctors appreciated (his oncologist was impressed and called the AI a member of the team).

Unfortunately his physical reserves were very drained at that point. He probably would have had another 6-12 months with his family if it wasn't for the disorganized mess of a care system that we have.

comment_text.value:
Interesting project, towards a decentralized Internet!

The heavy lifting is done in this function, pairing. You link your personal devices together, solid idea [0].

This Flipflop project relies on the Iroh library for NAT/Firewall puncturing, external address discovery and overlay networking. Connecting two 5G devices, without a coordinating central server is possible, but very hard. Iroh simply relies on a server which you could self-host. Cool stuff, we stress tested it a while ago and it somewhat worked.

NAT connectivity is unsolved. My university lab conducted one of the bigger puncturing studies a decade ago [1]. Recently, we also bought 40+ or something 4G and 5G SIM cards in Europe for puncturing [2]. My master student traveled Europe by bus to get these local SIM cards. He worked day-and-night to connect these weird symmetric 5G NAT filter boxes and got it working. Simple sync collision and birthday paradox brute force...
